transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been troubling you or what brings you in today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. It’s, um, it’s a bit complicated to explain where it all starts, I guess. I work as an IT systems manager, so I oversee a lot of infrastructure, network security, user databases, that sort of thing. It's a high-pressure job, sure, but what brings me in today is that I just keep getting these... these thoughts. 

It's like this constant, heavy dread that if I miss one setting—just a single configuration error, or one access rule that isn't perfectly locked down, or even just one tiny warning sign in the system logs—that someone could get seriously hurt. Or that the people relying on our systems could just lose absolutely everything. 

And the frustrating thing is, I mean, I know how these networks are built. I have a graduate degree in this, we have redundancies built into everything. The rational, logical part of my brain knows that it’s irrational to think the whole world will collapse because of one minor oversight. But it just doesn't matter what I logically know. The thought hits me so hard, like I am personally, entirely responsible for this massive impending catastrophe, and I just... I can’t just move on. I try to tell myself to let it go, to just close the laptop and trust the system, but my mind just gets completely stuck on the possibility of ruining people's lives and I can't let it go. It just loops and loops.

When these thoughts come up, do you find yourself doing certain things over and over—like checking logs repeatedly, changing settings multiple times, or going through specific mental rituals—to try to ease the anxiety or prevent the catastrophe from happening?

Yes. Yes, exactly that. It’s... it’s actually taking over my life, to be completely honest with you. When that dread hits, I can’t just sit there. I have to do something about it. I have to make sure. So I will pull up the deployment plans, for instance. And I don’t just look at them once. I will reread every single line, every IP address, every permission level, over and over again. And the audit logs... oh man, the audit logs. I’ll scroll through thousands of lines of code and user activity, looking for any anomaly, and if I lose my place, I have to start all over from the top of the hour or the top of the day, depending on how bad the feeling is. 

And it’s not just the systems at work, either. It bleeds into everything. I’ll check the server room door locks. I’ll pull the handle, then push it, then pull it again. Sometimes I have to count the steps in my head—like, one, two, three, four, lock is secure, system is safe—and I have to keep counting and checking until it feels... right. Until it feels 'safe.' If I get interrupted or if the number feels wrong, the anxiety just spikes all over again. I even find myself going back through old emails and Slack messages from weeks ago, rereading them repeatedly to make sure I didn't give someone the wrong instructions or authorize something I shouldn't have. 

It gets so bad that I’m often the last one at the office. I’ve stayed there for hours—three, four hours—after everyone else has gone home to their families. My wife calls and asks when I'm coming home, and I just tell her I'm finishing up, but the truth is I'm just stuck in this loop. Because if I try to stop, if I try to just pack up my bag and walk out the door before the checking feels complete, this overwhelming panic just washes over me. It’s like my chest tightens and I can’t breathe, and I just know something terrible is going to happen if I leave. So I sit back down, open the laptop, and start checking again.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms, including intrusive, distressing thoughts leading to repetitive behaviors (checking logs, door locks, emails, etc.) aimed at reducing anxiety, are highly consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The symptoms are time-consuming, cause significant distress, and impair functioning, which rules out other candidates like F43.22 (adjustment disorder with anxiety) and F32.9 (major depressive disorder, mild).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with recurrent, intrusive, and distressing obsessions related to catastrophic system failure and personal responsibility for preventing harm. These obsessions are accompanied by repetitive behaviors (e.g., checking logs, locks, counting) and mental acts (e.g., counting in head until 'feels right') performed in response to the obsessions in an effort to neutralize anxiety. The behaviors are not connected in a realistic way to what they are designed to neutralize, and they cause clinically significant distress and impairment in functioning, including prolonged work hours and interference with personal life.
